paper.title_en: Cryogenic CMOS Control Circuits for Scalable Quantum Computing Architecture
paper.abstract_en: The development of scalable quantum computing requires the development of classical control electronics capable of operating reliably under cryogenic conditions. Quantum processors currently depend on room-temperature control systems, which need multiple interconnect cables to connect their equipment. This study investigates cryogenic complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) circuits as a promising solution for scalable quantum computing control systems. The behaviour of CMOS devices at cryogenic temperatures is analysed in terms of carrier mobility, threshold voltage, leakage current, and switching characteristics, which all strongly influence circuit performance. The proposed system uses a hierarchical cryogenic control architecture, which distributes digital control and signal-generation blocks across different temperature stages to achieve reduced wiring overhead and improved system scalability. The researchers created a three-stage cryogenic CMOS ring oscillator to study how temperature affects oscillation frequency and propagation delay and power consumption and signal stability. This work presents a simulation-based analysis of cryogenic CMOS circuits using temperature-dependent device models. Cryogenic temperatures provide significant advantages, including increased carrier mobility for faster switching and reduced leakage current for lower static power, but they also introduce challenges such as threshold-voltage shifts, device variability, and modelling limitations that require cryogenic-aware design. The research demonstrates that cryogenic CMOS circuits function as efficient systems, which deliver compact control electronics that use minimal energy while maintaining scalability for superconducting qubit-based quantum computing systems.
